newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Turkey European aspirations run hot, EU stays cool.
newsitem.headline: Turkey European aspirations run hot, EU stays cool.

text.p: Turkey's inclusion at a meeting in Amsterdam for prospective future EU members was an historic moment in its more than 30-year quest for acceptance in the bloc, Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller said on Friday.
But the EU quickly made clear that the end of the secular Moslem state's long pilgrimage to win a place in Christian Europe is not yet in sight.

"The very fact that we are here today is an historic moment and an indication of the progress that has been made," Ciller told reporters after an EU briefing to 12 aspirant member countries to explain the state of the bloc after the recent Amsterdam summit.
Leaders from 10 eastern European candidates for EU entry were at the briefing, along with those from Cyprus and Turkey.
"Since 1963 we have been an applicant and for the first time we have achieved equal status with all the other applicants," Ciller said.
However, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok was quick to dampen any expectations that Turkey's membership claims, long stalled by Greek objections and human rights concerns, had advanced at all.
"The status quo has not changed in any way following today's meeting," he said, adding that Turkey had been invited on Friday because it was practical to talk to all aspirants together.

The eastern Europeans are all in line for EU expansion and anxiously waiting to see whether the bloc will decide to open talks with all of them at the same time, or on a staggered basis. Talks with Cyprus will start early next year.

Turkey, which has moved further than any other candidate states in forging economic and defence links with the EU, bitterly resents its continued treatment as a special case in discussions about enlargement.

"As we leave the old Cold War divisions in the distant past, we must ensure that new divisions based on culture, race or religion are not allowed to grow," Ciller told the EU briefing, according to a statement issued afterwards.
She emphasised that, as a NATO member and having implemented a customs union with the EU, Turkey felt entitled to a fair appraisal of its membership ambitions.

"Having brought a major contribution to Europe's defence...and pushed forward economic integration with the Union further than any other candidate, Turkey feels it has demonstrated its ability and willingness to assume the obligations of full membership."
And she said recent developments on the expansion issue did hold out hope of even-handed treatment.
"I am pleased to note that the conclusions adopted at the end of last week's European Council do not create artificial distinctions between the different candidates."

Recent political turmoil in Turkey, where secularist Mesut Yilmaz is attempting to form a new government without Ciller's True Path party, would not derail or even dilute Turkey's determination to play a part in Europe, she told the briefing.
"Whatever new coalition emerges, Turkey's basic commitment to Europe will continue undiminished. Full membership of the Union remains the choice of the vast majority of our people."

Turkey's EU ambitions have also long been thwarted by its historic rival and EU member Greece -- which links Turkey's membership to the question of Cyprus, divided since 1974 when Turkish forces invaded the island's north in response to a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia.
"We do want to see a solution in Cyprus," Ciller told reporters. "We want a solution as soon as possible."
Asked about the European Parliament's vocal criticism of Turkey's human rights situation, Ciller said it was addressing these concerns.
"What we are after is achieving a shelter of democracy and an umbrella of human rights. I am personally dedicated to that and we will continue in that direction," she said.
